{"target_language": "ta", "output_name": "tamil_summary", "text": "This is a summary of Chapter 6, Lines and Angles.

The chapter begins by showing why lines and angles matter in real life: building a model hut from bamboo sticks, drawing the plan of a tall building, studying light with ray diagrams, and finding the height of a tower or the distance of a ship from a lighthouse.

It then revises the basic terms. A part of a line with two end points is a line segment, and a part with one end point is a ray. Points on the same line are collinear. An angle is formed when two rays start from a common end point, called the vertex, and the rays are its arms. Angles are acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex. Two angles adding up to ninety degrees are complementary, and two adding up to one hundred eighty degrees are supplementary. Adjacent angles share a vertex and an arm, and a linear pair is formed when the non-common arms make a line.

The main results are the Linear Pair Axiom and Theorem 6.1. The axiom says that if a ray stands on a line, the two adjacent angles add up to one hundred eighty degrees, and its converse says that if two adjacent angles add up to one hundred eighty degrees, their non-common arms form a line. Theorem 6.1 proves that when two lines intersect, vertically opposite angles are equal. The chapter ends with worked examples using these ideas."}
